introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Economics 3 (0725), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2021. Duration: one and three quarter hours.**

Answer ANY THREE questions. All questions carry equal marks. You are advised to spend the first fifteen minutes reading the paper. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. Calculators are allowed.
enonce_intro_markdown:
"The economist's definition of perfect competition is different from the meaning of competition in everyday usage. The economist means that each individual, recognizing that his or her own quantities supplied or demanded are trivial relative to the market as a whole, acts on the assumption that his or her actions will have no effect on the market price....... Changes in market conditions, applying to all firms or all consumers, would change the equilibrium price and hence individual quantities demanded, but each individual could neglect any feedback from his or her actions to market price......."

*Curled from Economics by David Begg, Stanley Fischer and Rudiger Dornbusch, British Edition, 1984, page 164.*

(In the printed paper the words "the assumption that his or her actions will have no effect on the market price" are underlined.)

Perfect competition in the long run: entry shifts industry supply to the right and lowers the price (left); the firm produces at the minimum of AC with normal profit only (right); model answer to part (c)(ii).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Define perfect competition. (2 marks)

(ii) Given the underlined statement, what phrase adequately describes sellers and buyers in this market as concerns pricing? (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Definition.** Perfect competition is a market structure in which there are so many buyers and sellers, each so small relative to the whole market, that none can influence the price; the firms sell an identical (homogeneous) product, there is freedom of entry into and exit from the industry, and buyers and sellers have perfect knowledge of prices and market conditions. The price is determined by the interaction of total demand and total supply in the market.

**(ii) Phrase: "price takers".**

- The underlined statement says that each buyer and seller acts on the assumption that his or her own actions have no effect on the market price.
- Sellers and buyers therefore **take the price as given** by the market (they are price takers, not price makers): a firm can sell any quantity at the ruling market price, but if it charges more it loses all its customers.

questions.enonce_markdown: State four major characteristics of perfect competition. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Four major characteristics (any four, one mark each):

1. **A large number of buyers and sellers**, each too small to affect the market price (the firms are price takers).
2. **A homogeneous (identical) product:** the goods of different firms are perfect substitutes, so there is no branding or product differentiation and buyers have no reason to prefer one seller.
3. **Freedom of entry into and exit from the industry:** there are no barriers to entry (no patents, licences or very large start-up costs).
4. **Perfect knowledge:** buyers and sellers know the prices, costs and profits in the market, so a single price rules.
5. **Perfect mobility of factors of production** between uses and areas (so that firms can enter and leave).
6. **Firms aim at profit maximisation** (they produce where $MC = MR$), and there is no government intervention and no transport costs.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Using well labeled diagrams, illustrate the following:

(i) the situation of a perfectly competitive industry in the short run. (4 marks)

(ii) the normal long run situation of a firm in perfect competition. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The perfectly competitive industry in the short run.**

![fig-1](gce-al-economics-2021-p3-officiel-cameroun_exercice_2_fig_1.png)

*Left diagram (the industry).* Draw price on the vertical axis and the output of the industry on the horizontal axis. The industry demand curve $D$ slopes downwards and the industry supply curve $S$ (the sum of the marginal cost curves of all the firms) slopes upwards. They cross at the equilibrium price $P$ and the equilibrium quantity $Q$.

*Right diagram (a typical firm).* Draw the firm's cost and revenue curves on the same price scale.

- The firm faces a **horizontal demand curve at the market price $P$**: $P = AR = MR = D$.
- The $AC$ curve is U-shaped and the $MC$ curve is upward sloping and cuts $AC$ at its lowest point.
- The firm maximises profit where $MC = MR$ (with $MC$ rising), giving the output $q_1$.
- At $q_1$ the price $P$ is above the average cost $AC$, so the firm earns **abnormal (supernormal) profit** equal to $(P - AC) \times q_1$: the shaded rectangle.
- (In the short run the firm may also earn only normal profit, or make a loss, if the demand curve and price are lower; the diagram above shows the usual case in which a short-run profit is made.)

**(ii) The normal long-run situation of a firm.**

![fig-2](gce-al-economics-2021-p3-officiel-cameroun_exercice_2_fig_2.png)

- Abnormal profits attract new firms (free entry). The industry supply curve shifts to the right ($S_1$ to $S_2$) and the price falls from $P_1$ to $P_2$, until the abnormal profits have disappeared.
- In the long run the firm's demand curve ($P = AR = MR$) is **tangent to the lowest point of the $AC$ curve**, exactly where $MC$ cuts $AC$.
- The firm produces $q^*$ where $MC = MR$ and $AC = AR = P$: it earns **normal profit only** (zero abnormal profit), so there is no incentive for firms to enter or to leave.
- The firm produces at the minimum of its average cost (productive efficiency) and $P = MC$ (allocative efficiency).

questions.enonce_markdown:
Briefly explain why:

(i) abnormal profits are considered as "windfall" in perfect competition. (2 marks)

(ii) marginal revenue and average revenue are the same in perfect competition. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Abnormal profits are a "windfall" in perfect competition.**

- A windfall is an unexpected gain that is not the result of the firm's own lasting advantage. In perfect competition, abnormal profit arises from a temporary change outside the firm's control (for example a rise in demand or a fall in costs) that raises the market price.
- It cannot last: because there are no barriers to entry and knowledge is perfect, new firms are attracted into the industry, supply increases, the price falls and the abnormal profit disappears in the long run. Firms can only expect normal profit in the long run.

**(ii) Marginal revenue equals average revenue.**

- The firm is a price taker: it faces a perfectly elastic (horizontal) demand curve at the market price $P$, and it can sell as many units as it wishes at that price.
- Hence total revenue is $TR = P \times Q$, average revenue is $AR = \dfrac{TR}{Q} = P$, and the extra revenue from selling one more unit is $MR = \dfrac{\Delta TR}{\Delta Q} = P$.
- So $AR = MR = P$ at every level of output, and the curves coincide with the horizontal demand curve.
